# Grow the world's collective intelligence

[Explore open positions](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/quora)

Our mission

## Our mission

We build platforms that increase the pace at which humanity can grow its collective intelligence. This includes knowledge sharing among humans (Quora) and collaboration among humans and all kinds of AI (Poe). By focusing at the platform level, we are not creating knowledge or intelligence ourselves, but instead we focus on the most leveraged place for impact: removing friction and unlocking the potential in what everyone else has already learned, created, or trained. The more we enable collaborative thinking between humans, and between humans and AI, the faster ideas will diffuse, the faster technology will advance, and the faster the economy will grow. Our ultimate goal is to accelerate the ability for humanity as a whole, along with all artificial intelligence, to share knowledge, create technology, and work together to solve problems.

Our products

## Our products

![Image 2: Quora](https://www.quora.com/assets/product-quora.eb88f33def36.png)
Quora is a global knowledge sharing platform with hundreds of millions of monthly unique visitors, connecting writers who have knowledge across millions of topics with a global audience of readers who want to learn from their collective experience.

[Try Quora](https://www.quora.com/)![Image 3: Poe](https://www.quora.com/assets/product-poe.6317938e3e04.png)
Poe is a cloud workspace where millions of users run multiple AI agents on shared context and tools. One subscription, every frontier model, and the collaboration layer that makes them work together.

[Try Poe](https://poe.com/)

## Why Quora?

The remote nature of Quora allows us to attract a high talent global team that is unified in their excitement about the mission to grow the world's collective intelligence. If you are someone who thrives in a challenging and collaborative working team and values a flat, transparent, and meritocratic culture, you could be a great addition to our team. Here, growth and development are intentional. We invest in mentorship, feedback, and opportunities to take on ambitious work, and our colleagues are eager to share their journeys and help you chart yours.

![Image 4](https://www.quora.com/assets/donut-85.64e05dc43f62.png)85%

According to our 2025 engagement survey, 85% of our employees feel their opinion is valued when they share it.

![Image 5](https://www.quora.com/assets/donut-91.34d0f4385cac.png)91%

91% of our employees believe their work contributes to Quora's overall goal.

## Impact

We are a passionate, mission-driven team that celebrates success and offers everyone the opportunity to make a significant impact in their role. At Quora, our flat reporting structures ensure that all team members engage in meaningful work and have ample opportunities to expand their influence. We promote transparency to enhance the flow of information across all teams, eliminating silos so we can operate as one cohesive company, united in our mission every day.

> “There's always a meaningful challenge to solve, and I'm motivated by working on complex engineering problems with real world impact while continuing to improve my skills. Being trusted with real ownership has helped me grow alongside the systems I build, both technically and professionally.”

![Image 6: Julia Yan](https://www.quora.com/assets/person-julia-yan.c5dda01b1ba1.png)**Julia Yan**Software Engineer

> “I work with a diverse, engaging team that's flexible and encourages mutual learning. Quora's culture is transparent and open, allowing people to contribute to areas they find compelling, with ample opportunity for personal and professional development.”

![Image 7: Chinedu Osuigwe](https://www.quora.com/assets/person-chinedu-osuigwe.0d52ce1aa358.jpg)**Chinedu Osuigwe**Program Manager

## Benefits

At Quora we offer competitive compensation, including equity, along with comprehensive benefits for employees worldwide. As a remote company, we provide generous remote and wellness stipends, paid time off, including a shared winter shutdown, and benefits tailored to your country.

### General Benefits

*   Generous PTO & Holidays
*   Trainings, Licenses, & Books
*   Employee Activity Clubs (EAC)
*   Employee Equity

### Health

*   Comprehensive Medical Plans
*   Competitive Paid Parental Leave
*   Employee Assistance Program

### Remote First Perks

*   Work from (Almost) Anywhere
*   Flexible Working Schedule
*   Home Office & Wellness Stipend
*   Coworking Space Program

## Remote first

In 2020, we adopted a remote-first model to hire exceptional talent from around the world. Today, we continue to recruit across North America, Europe, Africa, and Asia ([see full list here](https://www.quora.com/eligible-countries)). To make this work well, we've intentionally designed how we operate, enabling us to stay fully remote even as many companies return to the office, either full time or in a hybrid model.

We rely on dedicated "coordination hours" to enable effective collaboration across time zones. Our daily [coordination hours](https://www.quora.com/quora-s-coordination-hours) run from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. Pacific Time. Of course, teammates work much more than these hours to deliver impact, but there is flexibility in when and how you get that work done. Whether you're working from home, traveling, or making use of our Coworking Space Program, you'll be part of a truly international community that values impact, teamwork, and the freedom to do challenging and meaningful work from wherever you can be the most productive.

## Interviewing at Quora

Our goal at Quora is to make the interview process both as friendly and as efficient as it can be. While each individual journey may vary, we strive to maintain consistency and fairness by following a similar process. Read on to learn about the different steps involved in our interview process and visit our Interviewing at Quora Space for more tips and tricks.

01 Apply+

Thank you for considering a career at Quora! Our hiring teams will carefully review your application and respond as soon as possible with any next steps. In the meantime, explore our careers page, LinkedIn, or even test your interviewing skills with one of the Bots on Poe.

02 Initial chats+

We're excited to have you in our interview process! One of our recruiters will be in touch soon to schedule a chat. We'll delve into your past experiences, discuss your career objectives, and make sure all of your questions are answered before you meet with the Hiring Manager. We're looking forward to getting to know you better and discovering how you could thrive in a role at Quora!

03 Practical stage+

To allow you to shine during the hiring process, we incorporate role-specific practical tasks (such as coding challenges, presentations, or mock scenarios) into our evaluation process. This will allow you to demonstrate your unique skills and expertise and ensure a more relaxed and relevant assessment experience.

By focusing on the practical skills required for each role, we're able to identify if we're a match for each other, regardless of your background or traditional credentials.

04 Virtual onsite loop+

Our virtual onsites typically occur over one or two days. During your onsite, you will meet a wide range of interviewers from across the company in a series of interviews. This stage allows you to showcase all aspects of your skills and gives you insight on how you will be working day-to-day.

05 Final conversations+

Following your final onsite interview, if you successfully progress to the next stage, you'll have the chance to connect with your future colleagues to answer any last minute questions or concerns. This final stage of the process provides you with a deeper understanding of the company culture and facilitates a seamless transition into your new role should you accept our offer.

06 Your first day!+

Welcome to Quora! We're so excited you'll be joining us. Leading up to your first day, you will receive some onboarding information from us to ensure you are all set up and ready to go for your first day. We can't wait to work with you!

## Be part of our mission

Discover exciting opportunities and grow with us.

[See open positions](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/quora)
Quora is proud to be an equal opportunity employer that values diversity. We do not discriminate on the basis of race, religion, color, national origin, gender, sexual orientation, age, marital status, veteran status, or disability status.

[![Image 1: Profile photo for Paul Michaels](https://qsf.cf2.quoracdn.net/-4-images.new_grid.profile_default.png-26-688c79556f251aa0.png)](https://www.quora.com/profile/Paul-Michaels-62)

Author has 281 answers and 1.1M answer views · [Updated 1y](https://www.quora.com/What-actor-or-actress-got-famous-without-any-ties-to-the-industry-and-just-plain-luck/answer/Paul-Michaels-62) · 

This man got his first role in a major film by plain luck, was the son of a social worker and a mechanic, with no ties to the film industry and no place at a posh private school to help grease the wheels - he has since gone on to become quite possibly the best actor from the UK -

I am of course talking about the incredibly talented Stephen Graham.

![Image 2](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-b23b660f70550c2d5945d577df9e864d)

Hi first major role was in Guy Ritchie’s Snatch - a role he only got as a result of tagging along with a friend of his who was auditioning for a role in the movie. Graham had no intention of auditioning, and when asked if he would, stated he was only there with a friend and couldn’t audition even if he wanted to because his dyslexia meant he could not read from the provided script.

He was allowed to improvise an audition and won a role in the film as “Tommy” alongside Brad Pitt and Jason Statham

![Image 3](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-0dd0bccec2be59129cda5e319539d0cf)

He followed this up with a role in Band of Brothers and Gangs of New York but got his true breakthrough role in 2006 - as the skinhead with neo-nazi leanings ‘Combo’ in the truly astounding “This is England” - ironically Stephen Graham is himself of mixed race origin, with Jamaican heritage on his fathers side.

![Image 4](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-a1b1686145362d1f6c9f27f6f342545b)

He would play this role three more times in the equally brilliant and harrowing This is England ‘86, ’88 and ‘90.

From here he has played everything from a Victorian Boxer in A Thousand Blows, to Al Capone in Boardwalk Empire, a Caribbean Pirate, a chef in Boiling Point and arguably, in his most powerful work yet, the father of a young boy accused of murder in Adolescence - a series that Graham also helped write and recently won three Emmys for.

![Image 5](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-fc0b4c72a5806777ad62f97c0be6dd5f)

This series also generated an Emmy win for the excellent Owen Cooper - a child actor who also does not have ties to the film industry. Graham had requested that they cast an unknown child actor from the North of England for the role.

3 June 1973 was when Amitabh and Jaya started their journey towards becoming one of Hindi cinema's best known partnerships. They married secretly in an almost quiet affair, right before leaving on their honeymoon to London. Amitabh had just witnessed a mega success with Zanjeer and was moving at the fastest possible speed.

Jaya was already an accomplished actress, having been a recipient of a National Award, whereas Amitabh was just creating his niche in the film industry. Soon, he rose to be one of the biggest Indian superstars of all times. Amidst all this unparalleled madness, Jaya chose to play the role of a more hands-on mother raising two children, Shweta and Abhishek, all the while being his anchor on the professional front too.

There was no looking back from there. They weathered the phase of Amitabh's superstardom in the 70s and then his stint as an MP. Then came the nineties with huge monetary issues. 

Followed by the near-fatal accident and multiple scandalous rumours of both their lives that continued to follow their journey of life. 

But their relationship not only withstood these trying times but continued on and on.

After more than fifty years, it doesn't feel like a story of a fairy tale anymore but of commitment, patience, understanding and persistence.

Amitabh and Jaya - two powerhouses who chose to pick and choose one another, again and again, with the turn of every age, and perhaps that is what makes them so remarkable.

Artificial intelligence is becoming one of the most powerful means of expanding human intellectual and creative capabilities. A scientist can consider more hypotheses, an engineer more technical solutions, a designer and architect more forms and concepts, a writer more ways of developing a thought or plot, and an artist and composer more images and creative possibilities.

Yet this is precisely where a paradox arises:

the more intellectual and creative work a person can delegate to a machine, the less of that work they need to perform themselves.

This does not mean that AI inevitably makes people less capable of thinking or creating something new. The risk arises when we systematically delegate to it precisely those operations that, when performed independently, develop and sustain our intellectual and creative abilities.

If AI formulates the problem, proposes hypotheses and concepts, generates options, constructs the argument, and helps bring the result to a finished form, the final product may improve while the user less and less often goes through the intellectual and creative process through which those abilities are exercised.

This raises the question: might people gradually turn from creators into selectors of what artificial intelligence creates?

Intellectual Output Is Not the Same as Intellectual Development

There is a fundamental difference between two ways of using AI:

"I have an idea. Help me test, expand, and improve it."

and

"Give me ideas from which I can choose the best one."

In the first case, AI primarily amplifies human creativity. In the second, it defines the space of ideas within which the user is left to choose.

With AI, we can write better, program faster, create more visual and musical variations, and find more scientific, engineering, and design solutions, while performing the operations that develop the corresponding abilities on our own less and less often.

The intellectual and creative power of the "human + AI" system may grow even as some human abilities weaken through insufficient use.

This does not necessarily mean the "dumbing down of humanity" or the decline of creativity. It is more accurate to speak of a change in the structure of human abilities. Some skills will become less important, others more important, and AI may free intellectual resources for the development of higher-level abilities.

The central question, therefore, is not whether people will think and create less, but what share of intellectual and creative activity they will delegate to the machine and how they will use the capacity this frees up.

The Illusion of Understanding and Cognitive Autopilot

AI creates a subtler problem as well: easy access to an explanation can be mistaken for understanding it oneself.

When a complex question instantly receives a clear and convincing answer, it is easy to feel: "Now I understand this." But reading an explanation is not the same as independently reconstructing causal connections, arguing for a conclusion, identifying a weak point, and applying knowledge in a new situation.

Receiving an answer and building one's own understanding are not the same thing.

Metacognition therefore becomes especially important — the ability to understand what we truly know, what we do not know, and where the limits of our competence lie.

A kind of cognitive autopilot emerges. The more reliable AI becomes, the less often we need to take full intellectual control ourselves. As long as the system works well, this is an enormous advantage. But it is important to preserve the ability to think independently when AI makes mistakes, works with incomplete data, or offers a convincing but incorrect solution.

Intellectual independence becomes a kind of cognitive security system.

But haven't technologies always freed people from mental work?

There is a strong historical objection to this idea. In Plato's Phaedrus, Socrates is presented as fearing that writing would weaken memory. Later, calculators freed us from some computation, computers from routine operations, and search engines from the need to remember countless facts.

Yet human thinking did not disappear. On the contrary, delegating some functions to technology allowed intellectual capacity to be directed toward more complex tasks.

It would be a mistake to treat every form of cognitive offloading as an intellectual loss.

Artificial intelligence had already demonstrated superiority over humans in certain intellectually demanding domains: symbolic milestones were Deep Blue's defeat of the world chess champion in 1997 and AlphaGo's victory over one of the strongest Go players in 2016. But these systems remained specialized. With the emergence of modern generative models, AI has become a widely used tool capable of participating not in a single narrow task, but in many different forms of everyday intellectual and creative activity.

The novelty of generative AI lies not in machines helping humans think and create for the first time, but in the ability of widely available systems to participate in many stages of intellectual and creative activity — from framing the problem and forming the initial concept to generating options, providing critique, making refinements, and producing the finished result.

The question, then, is not whether intellectual and creative work should be delegated to machines at all, but something else:

what can be delegated to AI in order to free people for further development, and what must continue to be done independently because it is precisely that activity that develops the abilities we want to preserve?

From Physical Culture to Cognitive Culture

Technological progress has freed people from a large share of physical labor, but it has not eliminated the body's need for exertion. If muscles and other physical capacities are systematically left unused, they weaken. Modern people therefore have to deliberately give their bodies what everyday life no longer provides enough of: walking, running, swimming, and exercise.

AI may confront us with a similar task in the intellectual and creative sphere. The more operations we delegate to machines, the less need there is to perform them ourselves. If certain abilities are systematically unused, they risk gradually weakening or failing to develop fully.

Thus, alongside physical culture, there may emerge a cognitive culture for the age of AI — the deliberate preservation and development of intellectual and creative abilities in a world where technology makes it increasingly unnecessary to use them independently.

This does not mean rejecting intellectual automation. Just as physical culture does not require giving up cars and walking everywhere again, cognitive culture does not require using AI less.

Its task is to divide intellectual and creative work wisely between people and machines.

The basic principle can be stated as follows:

delegate to the machine what frees people, but do not inadvertently delegate what develops them.

Sometimes a useful difficulty is not an obstacle to efficiency, but part of developing the ability itself.

There is therefore no point in artificially preserving every old skill. It is reasonable to delegate routine searches, data processing, technical formatting, and the exploration of alternatives to AI. But it is especially important to preserve the ability to independently formulate significant problems, create the initial concept, understand causal relationships, imagine new possibilities, critically evaluate what is proposed, set goals, and take responsibility for the final choice.

Selection Is Also an Intellectual and Creative Ability

At the same time, the very word "selector" should not mislead us.

Selection is a complex intellectual and creative activity. An editor, director, scientist, artist, architect, designer, or manager can create enormous value precisely through the ability to identify the best among many options. In a world of mass AI generation, this ability may become even more important.

The danger begins when selection becomes almost the only creative function, while problem formulation, the initial concept, the creation of alternatives, and even the criteria of evaluation are also delegated to the machine.

The same problem arises in visual art, music, architecture, and design: generating large numbers of options can gradually shift creative activity from independent creation toward selecting and refining what has been proposed.

High-quality selection requires knowledge, experience, understanding, taste, and one's own criteria.

The task, therefore, is not to set creativity against selection:

we must be able to choose the best from what AI creates without losing the ability to independently create new ideas, concepts, images, and solutions — including beyond the options proposed.

The Special Responsibility of Education

Here it is especially important to distinguish between an adult professional and a child.

An experienced professional can delegate part of the work to AI, drawing on already developed knowledge, professional intuition, and criteria. A child who delegates the formulation of thoughts, problem solving, or the creation of ideas and creative options to a machine too early may get less of the very practice needed to develop these abilities.

Hence an important principle:

before automating the use of an ability, a person must first be given the opportunity to develop that ability.

This does not mean isolating children from AI. On the contrary, the ability to work with it will become an important competence. But the nature of its use should depend on age and learning goals.

Education will increasingly need to distinguish between two things:

what a student can understand, create, and solve independently;

what the same student can do when augmented by AI.

Both competencies matter. The second must not conceal the absence of the first.

Perhaps even the meaning of a degree will change. In a world where a high-quality text, program, image, or design tells us less and less about the creator's own abilities, a strong academic credential may become a kind of certificate of intellectual and creative independence.

When Answers Become Cheaper, Questions Become More Valuable

AI is making good answers increasingly accessible. But this does not necessarily diminish the role of human intelligence — its value may shift to another level.

When a good answer is available to almost everyone, the ability to understand what is worth asking in the first place becomes especially valuable.

To see a problem others have missed. To question initial assumptions. To connect distant fields of knowledge. To understand which of hundreds of answers truly matters.

A good question does not arise from an intellectual vacuum. It requires knowledge, perceptiveness, and one's own understanding of the subject. The external availability of knowledge therefore does not eliminate the need to have knowledge within oneself.

AI is becoming ever better at helping answer the question "how?" But questions such as "what should be done?", "why?", "for what purpose?", and "what kind of future should we consider desirable?" are bound up with human needs, values, and goals.

An answer expands knowledge within a given space. A genuinely new question can change the very space of inquiry.

In art and design, there is a closely related question: not only "which option is better?" but "what image, form, or direction has not yet been proposed at all?"

When There Are More Options but Less Diversity

There is another paradox.

AI is trained on vast bodies of human culture. If millions of people use similar systems at the earliest stage of creating ideas, images, and concepts, the ways solutions are sought — and even the ways creative problems are framed — may gradually converge.

At the same time, it would be a mistake to regard AI as incapable of originality. Generative systems can themselves create unexpected combinations and expand the creative possibilities of individual users.

Individual creativity assisted by AI may therefore even become stronger. The problem arises at another, collective level: the outputs of many people may become somewhat more similar to one another.

The risk, then, is not necessarily a reduction in the creative possibilities of an individual creator. It is that the creativity of many people may become extraordinarily diverse within a space shaped largely by similar systems, while venturing beyond that space less often.

AI-assisted content then becomes part of the information environment with which future generations of people and subsequent AI systems interact. This can potentially create a feedback loop of intellectual and creative standardization.

Such an outcome is not inevitable. AI can, on the contrary, expose users to ideas, cultures, styles, and fields of knowledge they might never have reached on their own. That is precisely why it is important to preserve independent sources of human originality — personal experience, knowledge, cultural diversity, individual perception, unusual associations, and independent problem formulation.

A paradox emerges that may become one of the defining features of the AI age:

each person's creative possibilities may expand, while the diversity of what many people produce may grow much more slowly.

In other words, one risk of the AI age may be not a shortage of new ideas and images, but their unprecedented abundance within increasingly similar intellectual and creative frameworks.

What Should We Do?

Three principles are enough to begin with.

First: your own concept before machine-assisted expansion. In important intellectual and creative tasks, first formulate your own position, idea, image, or at least an initial concept, and only then turn to AI.

Second: use AI not only as a generator, but also as an opponent. Ask: "What have I overlooked?", "Where is the weakness in my idea?", "What alternatives exist?", "How can I move beyond what has already been proposed?"

Third: regularly test your own intellectual and creative independence. Can I explain the answer in my own words? Can I independently create an initial concept or solve at least the main parts of the task? It is useful to continue doing some intellectual and creative work regularly without AI.

At the same time, the final choice and responsibility should remain ours. "AI suggested it" must not become a new way of avoiding responsibility.

The task is not to use artificial intelligence less. The task is to use it at a higher level.

Conclusion

AI may become the greatest intellectual and creative amplifier in history. But the power of the "human + AI" system may grow at the same time as the need to use certain human abilities independently declines.

One response to this challenge may be cognitive culture — a conscious division of intellectual and creative activity between people and machines, in which the growth of AI's capabilities is accompanied by the development of human abilities rather than the gradual abandonment of their independent use.

As answers become more accessible, good questions become more valuable. As the number of available options becomes almost limitless, the ability to move beyond what has been proposed grows in value. As AI becomes ever better at answering "how?", questions such as "what?", "why?", "for what purpose?", and "what kind of future do we want to create?" take on special importance.

A selector mainly chooses from what is offered; a creator is able not only to choose, but also to create something new independently — including beyond the options proposed.

Perhaps one of the main crossroads of the twenty-first century will lie not between humanity and artificial intelligence, but within each of us. The central task of cognitive culture is to preserve the human being as a creator in a world where being a selector will become much easier.

And perhaps, a century from now, the central question about the age of AI will not be:

"How intelligent did machines become?"

but:

"What happened to the human being when machines became intelligent?"

A zillion celebrities have gone to Harvard. My dad was friends with the heir to Aga Kahn III, and is now Aga Kahn IV. There’s a funny story about him bailing my father out of jail with a $1000 bill, but it’s too long to tell.

I got to meet him when my dad went to a reunion when I was about 15. I can’t remember who else he knew.

Franklin Delano Roosevelt famously got a ‘D’ in his government class.

I was friendly with Conan O’Brien, although not close. His best friend was dating my roommate, so he was often looming over me (he’s really tall). He’s hilarious. Like you can’t stop laughing the entire time he’s speaking hilarious. He did very well, but I can’t remember his exact degree, probably Magna.

I studied a lot with Tom Morello for an English History class, the guitarist from Rage Against the Machine. He was in an Honors major (we call them “concentrations”), so he graduated cum laude at least.

I didn’t get along with the woman who is now the Empress of Japan, Masako Owada. She was jealous of my boyfriend, and REALLY DIDN’T LIKE ME. But we both were in the Japan Club, so we spent a lot of time together. She gossiped about me in Japanese right in front of me, because she knew I couldn’t understand her. My boyfriend could understand her. She graduated Magna cum Laude.

I also know a lot of people who are famous within their field, but not to the general public. My husband once said about my anecdotes, “So going to Harvard is about meeting a lot of people who become semi-famous.” Which is a pretty good summation.

My junior year at Harvard, I took "Intro to Directing", taught by David Wheeler, who was Resident Director at the American Repertory Theater. For that class we would have to prepare scenes for our peers that would then serve as food for discussion and help us explore how the directorial choices we had made shaped the dramatic movement of our pieces.

Matt was in my class, and one day he brought in an original piece he had been working on. It involved a scene in a shrink's office and centered on a very bright kid turning the tables on his therapist by means of analyzing a painting hanging on his wall. Matt played the troubled kid in what later became known as Good Will Hunting, the movie he wrote and produced with Ben Affleck that helped launch both their careers.

I remember being very impressed with the sophistication of the dramatic premise and by how well the scene allowed the spoken text to reveal character and set the stage for the antagonistic relationship between the pair. I was equally impressed by his acting chops. Most of us in that class were aspiring directors, not actors, so to witness quality acting among us was a rare thrill. He was very natural, inhabiting the role with his entire body—understated but powerfully effective at the same time.

I took note, and after class, asked if he would act in an original scene I had been working on. The scene, an autobiographical account drawn from my childhood, depicted that moment, that loss of innocence, that takes place between two siblings as they listen to their parents, in the throes of a divorce, arguing through the wall of their bedroom. Matt played my older brother. The scene played out from our respective places in our bunk beds—me on top, he on the bottom. We didn't have these props in our classroom, so we improvised by arranging ourselves on a desk—me lying across the top, he on the floor beneath.

I think we had one quick rehearsal before bringing it into class. He knew the script cold, and as we acted out the piece, I literally got goosebumps - He intuitively understood what the scene was about. My direction was minimal, yet he got to the heart of what it meant to be two frightened boys, realizing for the first time that their parents may not always be there and realizing that they were on their own to support each other and provide for their emotional well being.

The piece was well received—it was positively praised as being very "cinematic"—I thanked Matt profusely and felt oddly connected because I felt he had readily understood where I was coming from.

A few years later, on my way to my bank in Harvard Square, I saw there was a big todo right outside of Au Bon Pain. The Square had been turned into a film set. When I peered through the reflectors, I was delighted to spy Matt, sitting at one of the wrought-iron tables, waiting as the crew raced about to prepare for the next shot.

I made my way over to him to congratulate him. I don't know if he placed my face, but he was gracious nonetheless. I lingered outside the cordon to see a take. I was elated to see they had given a homeless man who distributed Spare Change, a magazine written and edited by the homeless, a cameo role. He had become a fixture of the Square, infecting everyone with his good cheer and friendly manner as he boomed "Young man!" to all passers by, waking them up from their reverie as they drifted through the Square.

To some, it seemed that Matt became an overnight success. The media loves to seize on the compelling aspect of this narrative, but the truth is that Matt had long been working at his craft with dogged determination. When he finally got into a position to exhibit his talent before people who were in position to help him, his success was a foregone conclusion.

Unremarkable.

I was at Harvard at the same time as Natalie Portman (1999-2003). My roommate took a seminar with her (a small five-person class that met for a few hours each week) in which they read War and Peace. He said she was pretty down-to-earth, and academically focused. Pretty much what you'd expect from a someone who's chosen to scale back a successful acting career for a few years to pursue a degree.

I saw her around campus occasionally - she lived in the same dorm as a girl I dated that year, but nothing noteworthy ever really happened. That entryway in Grays was somehow higher security, though I'm not clear on the details. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Harvard_dormitories#Grays_Hall

She decided not to live in Harvard dorms during her last two years at the school, which was pretty unusual (more than 90% of students stay in the residential houses all 4 years). I think I never saw her between freshman year (when I saw her occasionally in our ridiculous Harry Potter-style dining hall[1]) and graduation.

People talked about Natalie Portman freshman year, but pretty much lost interest after that. She wasn't a big presence, didn't throw big parties, and after Star Wars: Episode I, didn't show up in any big feature films except the 2002 (end of junior year), Star Wars Episode II.

Interesting side note. Natalie Portman's info wasn't searchable in Harvard's main directory, but most students' info was. A friend of mine (also named Natalie) said that she received a couple emails every month from people who assumed Ms. Portman was using a different last name at school, looked up all the Natalies and emailed them for "advice about going to Harvard, being an actress, etc."

[1] Here's a picture of that dining hall. Yes, it seemed ridiculous when we were there. No, it didn't seem like Harry Potter, since none of the movies had been made yet.

The **[Pennsylvania State Capitol](link_33)** is located in [Harrisburg](link_21). The building was designed by [Joseph Miller Huston](link_22) and completed in 1906 in a [Beaux-Arts](link_23) style with decorative [Renaissance](link_24) themes. It houses the legislative chambers for the [Pennsylvania General Assembly](link_25), the Harrisburg chambers for the [Supreme Court](link_26) and [Superior Court of Pennsylvania](link_27), and the offices of [the state's governor](link_28) and [lieutenant governor](link_29). The capitol project was the subject of a [graft](link_30) scandal, as the construction and furnishing cost three times more than the General Assembly had appropriated for the project. The Pennsylvania State Capitol is often referred to as a "palace of art" because of its many sculptures, murals, and stained-glass windows, most of which are Pennsylvania-themed or were made in Pennsylvania. The building was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](link_31) in 1977 and designated a [National Historic Landmark](link_32) in 2006. _(**[Full article...](link_33)**)_

# Donate

# Donate to the   
Wikimedia Foundation

### Wikipedia is the world’s largest encyclopedia — and it’s yours! Every donation helps keep Wikipedia free and open for people across the globe.

**Only 2% of Wikipedia readers give, so your donation really counts.**

Amount

 $ 

Frequency Just once Give monthly Annual 

Donate now

[Tax deductibility information](link_54)

## Ways to give

![Image 5: Illustration of a smiling woman holding a heart, on a teal circular background.](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/themes/shiro/assets/src/svg/give-icon-friendship.svg)
### [Give once](link_55)

Make an impact with a quick and secure online donation today.

![Image 6: Illustration of a figure surrounded by paper airplanes flying in different directions, on an orange circular background.](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/adapted-wikipedia20symbol-icon-friendship.svg)
### [Give monthly](link_17)

Become a monthly donor to help support Wikipedia all year round.

![Image 7: Illustration of a circular burst of confetti, on a yellow circular background.](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Group-28.svg)
### [Give yearly](link_56)

Donating once a year is a small commitment that makes a huge difference.

## More ways to support our work

### [Give by mail](link_57)

Because we know that not everyone prefers to donate online.

### [Donate via bank account](link_58)

Find out how to donate via your bank account from anywhere in the world.

### [Donor-advised fund (DAF)](link_59)

Unlock tax benefits by directing your donation via your Donor-Advised Fund (DAF).

### [Stock donation](link_60)

Maximize your impact and benefit from tax savings.

### [Legacy gift](link_20)

Make a difference for generations to come.

### [Individual Retirement Account (IRA)](link_61)

### [CGA](link_62)

### [Workplace giving](link_63)

Involve your employer and increase the impact of your donation

### [Endowment gift](link_64)

### [Visit the Wikipedia store](link_65)

From apparel to home goods, stationery, and more—find the perfect item to show your support.

* * *

## Already a donor?

Thank you for your generous support. It really makes a difference. For information on how to manage your recurring donation, please click below, or contact [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org).

[Manage your donation](link_21)

## What your donation makes possible

Wikipedia is not funded through advertising, and we don’t sell your data for profit. Instead, we rely on donors — people who find value in the free knowledge and resources we provide. This means Wikipedia remains neutral, trusted, and free from commercial interests. Watch our video to learn more.

[Video 1](link_66)

## Where your donation goes

Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](link_67) for more information about our financial health.

### Investment in Technology 45%

Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

### Support for Volunteers 32%

The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

### General and Administrative Expenses 11%

Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

### Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 12%

Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

* * *

## Thank you

We appreciate each and every person who chooses to become a Wikimedia Foundation donor! You are the key to making this important work possible. Thank you. We also offer a special acknowledgement to our Benefactors — people who give $1,000 or more. We proudly list our [Benefactors here](link_68).

“Thank you for your thoughtful approach to technology and for ensuring that people remain at the heart of Wikipedia’s mission.”

**Donor**

●**_United States of America_**

“It is an honour to be able to contribute to Wikipedia, which I always try to refer to as the eighth wonder of the world.”

**Donor**

●_The Netherlands_

“[Wikipedia is] one of the last bastions of free, open and collaborative internet. Keep up the good fight!”

**Donor**

●_Brazil_

“I believe that open knowledge is the foundation of true progress, and platforms like Wikipedia don’t just inform us — they empower us. That belief will stay with me forever.”

**Donor**

●_United Kingdom_

“Free knowledge for all should be our main treasure as a society… Thank you for a project that will transcend generations.”

**Donor**

●_Colombia_

* * *

## Still have questions?

Please find answers to our most frequently asked questions below. If you’re unable to find what you are looking for there, you can browse our [general FAQs](link_11), or get in touch using [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org).

### Are my donations tax deductible?

The Wikimedia Foundation has 501(c)(3) tax exempt status in the United States. Our tax-exempt status varies according to the laws of each country. Donations to the Wikimedia Foundation are likely not tax-deductible outside the USA. Please see our [tax deductibility](link_54) page for more details.

### What is your donor privacy policy?

We are committed to protecting the privacy rights of our supporters and will never sell, trade, or rent your nonpublic personal information. Please see our [Donor privacy policy](link_69) for full details.

### How secure is an online donation?

The Wikimedia Foundation donation pages are extremely secure and powered by [GlobalSign](link_70). After clicking on a fundraising banner or following a donation link, the page you’re taken to is on a secured site (https); all information is encrypted and handled following the highest standard of data protection.

We would also like you to know that we neither process nor store credit card details or bank information. Instead, we work closely with third party payment processors affiliated with banks to process donations. Please also note that when you transfer to a partner site – if you are donating via Apple Pay, Google Pay, or PayPal, for example – we do not store your login credentials and the full donation process is done from your account on their secure site.

### How can I update my recurring gift?

You may pause, update, or cancel your recurring donation via your donor portal. [Please click here](https://donorpreferences.wikimedia.org/index.php?title=Special:DonorPortal&wmf_medium=wmfSite&wmf_source=113#/login) to log in with the email address you used to set up your donation.

If you donate by credit/debit card, in some cases credit card processors will notify us when card details (including expiration date) are updated, to ensure the donation is not interrupted. If you have questions about this, please contact your credit card provider for more information.

Please note that if you donate via PayPal, you may need to manage your donation directly via your PayPal account.

If you encounter any issues or have any questions, please reach out to our Donor Relations team at [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org) and they will be happy to assist. **Please do not include your credit card number or other financial information when contacting us.**

Due to the volume of inquiries we receive, we use Zendesk as a donor response platform. By emailing [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org), you understand that your information will be processed by the Zendesk Group in accordance with Zendesk’s terms. Users from the following countries should consult Section A of Zendesk’s privacy policy for more information about Zendesk’s country-specific practices: Australia, Brazil, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and Singapore.

[View all frequently asked questions](link_54)

## Don’t just take our word for it

Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (Formerly Guidestar), and Charity Navigator has awarded us its highest rating of four stars.

Title: Wikimedia

URL Source: https://www.wikimedia.org/

Published Time: Mon, 28 Sep 2026 15:41:33 GMT

Markdown Content:
![Image 1](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/wikimedia_logo.png)

Welcome! The Wikimedia movement is a global community of people, projects, and activities working together to create and share knowledge freely. Join us in making all knowledge available to everyone, everywhere.

![Image 2](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/welcome-image.svg)

Our Projects

Our projects are the core of the [Wikimedia movement](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:MyLanguage/Wikimedia_movement). All major projects are operated by the [Wikimedia Foundation](https://wikimediafoundation.org/), and the content is collaboratively developed by over 260,000 users worldwide using the [MediaWiki](https://www.mediawiki.org/) software.

Reference

[![Image 3](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikipedia-logo_sister.svg) Wikipedia The Free Encyclopedia](https://www.wikipedia.org/)[![Image 4](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wiktionary-logo_sister.svg) Wiktionary Free dictionary](https://www.wiktionary.org/)[![Image 5](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikiquote-logo_sister.svg) Wikiquote Free quote compendium](https://www.wikiquote.org/)[![Image 6](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikibooks-logo_sister.svg) Wikibooks Free textbooks](https://www.wikibooks.org/)

Collections

[![Image 7](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Commons-logo_sister.svg) Commons Free media collection](https://commons.wikimedia.org/)[![Image 8](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikisource-logo_sister.svg) Wikisource Free content library](https://www.wikisource.org/)[![Image 9](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikiversity-logo_sister.svg) Wikiversity Free learning resources](https://www.wikiversity.org/)[![Image 10](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikispecies-logo_sister.svg) Wikispecies Free species directory](https://www.wikispecies.org/)

Technology

[![Image 11](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikidata-logo_sister.svg) Wikidata Free knowledge base](https://www.wikidata.org/)[![Image 12](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikifunctions-logo_sister.svg) Wikifunctions Free function library](https://www.wikifunctions.org/)[![Image 13](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/MediaWiki-logo_sister.svg) MediaWiki Free & open wiki software](https://www.mediawiki.org/)

Guides

[![Image 14](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Wikivoyage-logo_sister.svg) Wikivoyage Free travel guide](https://www.wikivoyage.org/)

Collaboration

[![Image 15](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/Meta-Wiki-logo_sister.svg) Meta-Wiki Community coordination & documentation](https://meta.wikimedia.org/)

The [Wikimedia Foundation](https://wikimediafoundation.org/) is the non-profit organization that hosts all Wikimedia projects and supports communities all over the world who create and curate freely accessible content.

![Image 16](https://www.wikimedia.org/portal/wikimedia.org/assets/img/puzzle-globe.svg)

Your donation protects the human right to free and open knowledge for everyone.

[Donate now](https://donate.wikimedia.org/?wmf_medium=wikimediaPortal&wmf_campaign=wikimediaPortalBtn&wmf_source=wikimediaPortalBtn)

Contact

Questions about the Wikimedia Foundation or Wikimedia projects? Get in touch.

[Contact](https://wikimediafoundation.org/about/contact/)

# Donor advised funds (DAF)

# **Support Wikipedia with a gift from a Donor-Advised Fund**

### When you give through your Donor-Advised Fund (DAF), you’re not just making a donation, you’re also combining favorable tax benefits with the flexibility to support your preferred causes.

## How do I make a DAF gift to the Wikimedia Foundation?

There are two simple ways to recommend a grant from your DAF to the Wikimedia Foundation, Inc:

### **Make a gift via DAFpay**

You can now give to the Wikimedia Foundation from your Donor-Advised Fund in just three clicks using DAFpay via this button:

#### **Why donate via DAFpay?**

*   Avoid lost checks & mailing delays
*   Track your gift from initiation through to fund receipt
*   Notify us of your donation instantly, so we can say thanks

_Please note grants through DAFpay are temporarily unavailable for Vanguard Charitable, you can still recommend grants directly through the Vanguard Charitable website._

* * *

### Make a gift via your financial institution

Alternatively, if you’d prefer to make a gift via your financial institution, your advisor can mail the grant with your name, fund name, contact information, and check to:

**Organization Name**: Wikimedia Foundation  
**EIN:**20-0049703  
**Mailing Address:** Wikimedia Foundation, PO Box 98204, Washington, DC 20090

Please include your full name, fund name, email, or mailing address when recommending a grant so we can ensure you received an acknowledgment. For any questions please contact us at [benefactors@wikimedia.org](mailto:benefactors@wikimedia.org).

* * *

## Still have questions?

Please find answers to our most frequently asked questions below. If you’re unable to find what you are looking for there, you can browse our [general FAQs](https://wikimediafoundation.org/who-we-are/frequently-asked-questions/), or get in touch using [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org).

### **What is a Donor-Advised Fund (DAF)?**

A Donor-Advised Fund is a charitable investment account meant for supporting the charitable organizations that matter most to you.

The funds grow tax-free, and you can then recommend grants from the DAF to qualified charities over time.

DAFs are the fastest-growing charitable giving vehicle in the United States because they are one of the easiest and most tax-advantageous ways to give.

For more information about how to establish a DAF, please contact a financial advisor/fund administrator at a sponsoring organization such as a financial institution or community foundation for assistance in setting up a DAF for the first time.

### **Why is a DAF beneficial to you?**

*   **Tax Benefits:** You receive an immediate tax deduction for your contribution and avoid capital gains taxes on any appreciated assets donated.
*   **Simplicity and Cost-Effectiveness:**DAFs are simpler and less expensive to administer than a private foundation, with lower compliance requirements.
*   **Flexibility:** You can make contributions to your DAF at any time and recommend grants over time, allowing you to “bundle” your charitable giving.
*   **Legacy:** You build a tradition of family philanthropy

### **Can I name the Wikimedia Foundation as a beneficiary of my Donor-Advised Fund in my will?**

Yes, naming the Wikimedia Foundation as a beneficiary of your donor-advised fund is a powerful way to ensure your values live on. Simply ask your fund advisor how to name Wikipedia as a beneficiary. And if you have any questions, feel free to reach out to Jess Schoenig at [legacy@wikimedia.org](mailto:legacy@wikimedia.org) or call (415) 541-2148 x6740. We’re happy to help!

### How do Donor-Advised Fund tax deductions work?

**Immediate benefit:** You get an immediate tax deduction when you donate to a DAF-sponsoring organization. The deduction applies for the tax year in which the contribution is made to the DAF, not when the funds are distributed to a charity. (You don’t get an additional tax deduction when the DAF makes a grant to a charity.)

[View all frequently asked questions](https://wikimediafoundation.org/give/donor-frequently-asked-questions/)

_**Please note:** This page is for informational purposes only. It does not contain financial or investment advice. Please consult a certified tax professional in your locality to determine if your donation is tax-deductible._

## Celebrate Wikipedia’s 25th birthday

Mark this milestone by paying tribute to the hundreds of thousands of people that edit, write, and fact check the backbone of knowledge on the internet.

[Join the party](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wikipedia25/)

## By the numbers

Wikipedia is the backbone of the internet’s knowledge. From students to chatbots, everyone learns from it.

![Image 5](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/wiki-globe.svg)

324

With over **67 million articles**, in **300+ languages**, Wikipedia is the home of trusted information online.

![Image 9](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/wiki-mobile.svg)
Wikipedia is the only website among the **top 10** most visited that is hosted by a nonprofit organization.

## Built for people, by people

Wikipedia is built by nearly 250,000 volunteers from all kinds of backgrounds. They edit articles, check facts, fix code, and help make the internet’s knowledge better. Meet some of them.

[](https://www.mapbox.com/)

![Image 19](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-WikiSG_Headshots_Taufik.jpg)
### **Taufik Rosman**

_Malaysia_

The 2023 Wikimedian of the Year, Taufik has been editing since he was 8 years old. He has expanded the Malay Wiktionary with nearly 11,000 changes. “Each of our contributions matters greatly,” Taufik says.

![Image 20](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Siobhan_Leachman_at_BioBlitzWBN_1.jpg)
### **Siobhan Leachman**

_New Zealand_

Siobhan expands English Wikipedia with knowledge about notable women in biodiversity and natural history. Thanks to her, Wikipedia has information about all of New Zealand’s 1,800 endemic moth species.

![Image 21](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Armine_Aghayan-Flisch.jpg)
### **Armine Aghayan-Flisch**

_Switzerland_

Writing a Wikipedia article each day for a hundred straight days is a feat. Arminé has done it thirteen times on the Armenian Wikipedia, while also uploading over 20,000 open-licensed images.

![Image 22](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Le_Burex_de_WikiCiv.jpg)
### **Donatien Kangah**

_Côte d’Ivoire_

The most visible part of Donatien’s French Wikipedia work is in the site’s coverage of African football. But behind the scenes, Danatien also runs an organization that expands Wikipedia’s knowledge of Côte d’Ivoire.

![Image 23](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-The_Photographer_User_in_Humboldt_Peak.jpg)
### **Wilfredo Rodríguez**

_Canada_

Prolific photographer Wilfredo has shared over 50,000 images with Wikimedia projects. Many come from his home country of Venezuela to preserve its beauty for the world’s benefit.

![Image 24](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Equipo_de_Wikipedistas_en_El_Salvador.jpg)
### **Ellie Méndez**

_El Salvador_

Ellie has collaborated with multiple El Salvadorean cultural institutions to expand Wikipedia’s coverage of women’s sports in Spanish and train people in updating the site.

![Image 25](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/512px-Monica_Bonilla.jpg)
### **Mónica Paola Bonilla-Parra**

_Colombia_

As the head of Wikimedia Colombia, Mónica works to encourage people to share knowledge on Wikipedia. “There are no limits to participating and contributing,” she says. “If you don’t do it, who will?”

![Image 26](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Wikisource_Conference_2025_Day_3_Denpasar_February_2025_086.jpg)
### **Alberto Leoncio**

_Brazil_

Most work on Wikipedia happens behind the scenes and is performed by volunteers like Alberto. The time Alberto spends on technical tasks makes life easier for all other Portuguese Wikipedia editors.

![Image 27](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/512px-Wikiar2022_0034_cropped.jpg)
### **Alaa Najjar**

_MENA region_

Alaa’s nearly 600,000 edits on Wikimedia projects have expanded the sites’ knowledge of medicine, anatomy, and biology. In thanks, he received the prestigious 2021 Wikimedian of the Year award.

![Image 28](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Nkem_Osuigwe_3.jpg)
### **Nkem Osuigwe**

_Nigeria_

Nkem is a connector: she brings volunteer Wikimedia editors and librarians from Africa together. Her work in organizing the first African Librarians Week generated nearly 28,000 improvements on Wikipedia.

![Image 29](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Ananya_Mondal_-_WLM.jpg)
### **Ananya Mondal**

_India_

A clinical nutritionist by trade, Ananya singlehandedly spearheaded an initiative to upload more images of butterflies onto Wikimedia projects. She’s since inspired people to upload over 15,000 new photos.

![Image 30](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Netha_Hussain-070A3987.jpg)
### **Netha Hussain**

_Sweden_

Netha uses her expertise as a doctor to ensure medical content on Wikipedia is accurate, well-sourced, and easily understood—from COVID-19 content during the pandemic to documenting misinformation around women’s health.

![Image 31](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/512px-Rosie_at_Wikimania_2023_6.jpg)
### **Rosie Stephenson-Goodknight**

_United States_

Rosie co-founded the Women in Red project, which is spearheading an effort to increase Wikipedia’s biographies about women in English. So far, they’ve added over 200,000 articles.

![Image 32](https://wikimediafoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/1024px-Andrew_Lih.jpg)
### **Andrew Lih**

_United States_

Long-time Wikipedian Andrew wrote The Wikipedia Revolution, a foundational book on the history of Wikipedia. Over the last two decades, he’s made over 760,000 improvements across Wikimedia projects.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Free licensed works in any field

For understanding how free content works on Wikipedia, see [Wikipedia:Free content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Free_content "Wikipedia:Free content").

"Free use" redirects here. For the fetish, see [Sexual objectification §Free use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_objectification#Free_use "Sexual objectification").

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Discussing_Creative_Commons_licensing_in_Khmer.jpg/330px-Discussing_Creative_Commons_licensing_in_Khmer.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Discussing_Creative_Commons_licensing_in_Khmer.jpg)

The logo on the computer screen represents a Creative Commons license, while the paper explains (in Khmer) that the image is free content.

**Free content**, **libre content**, or **open content** (also called **free information**, **libre information**, **open information**) is any kind of [creative work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_work "Creative work"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_content#cite_note-1) such as a [work of art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_of_art "Work of art"), a [book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book "Book"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_content#cite_note-2) a [software program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_software "Free software"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_content#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_content#cite_note-4) or any other creative [content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_(communication) "Media (communication)") for which [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright") and other legal limitations on usage, modification and distribution are minimal.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
This article is about the online encyclopedia. For Wikipedia's home page, see Main Page. For the history of Wikipedia, see History of Wikipedia. For the English-language Wikipedia, see English Wikipedia. For other uses, see Wikipedia (disambiguation).
Wikipedia
The Wikipedia logo depicts a globe made out of puzzle pieces with glyphs from various writing systems.

Wikipedia[e] is a free online encyclopedia written and maintained by a community of volunteer editors, known as Wikipedians, through open collaboration and the wiki software MediaWiki. Founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001, Wikipedia has been hosted since 2003 by the Wikimedia Foundation, an American nonprofit organization funded mainly by donations from readers.[1] Wikipedia is the largest and most read reference work in history.[2][3]

Initially available only in English, Wikipedia has grown to over 300 languages and is one of the world's most visited websites as of 2026. The English Wikipedia, with over 7 million articles, remains the largest of the editions, which together comprise more than 68 million articles and attract more than 1.5 billion unique device visits and 13 million edits per month (about five edits per second on average) as of April 2024.[4] As of December 2025, over 25% of Wikipedia's traffic comes from the United States, while Japan accounts for nearly 7%, and the United Kingdom, Germany, and Russia each represent around 5%.[5]

Wikipedia has been praised for its internal structure and culture, enabling the democratization of knowledge, and for its extensive coverage on various topics. The encyclopedia has also been criticized for systemic bias, such as a gender bias against women and a geographical bias against the Global South.[6][7] The reliability of Wikipedia was frequently criticized in the 2000s, but has received greater praise from the late 2010s onward.[2][8] Censorship of Wikipedia by national governments has ranged from censoring specific pages to the entire site, sometimes due to its criticism of the government, or for content considered blasphemous.[9][10][11] Wikipedia articles on breaking news are accessed as sources for up-to-date information by many.[12][13]

History
Main article: History of Wikipedia
Nupedia
Main article: Nupedia
Wikipedia founders Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger

Various collaborative online encyclopedias were attempted before Wikipedia's launch, but with limited success.[14] Wikipedia began as a complementary project for Nupedia, a free online English-language encyclopedia project whose articles were written by experts and reviewed under a formal process.[15] It was founded on March 9, 2000, under the ownership of Bomis, a web portal company. Its main figures were Bomis CEO Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger, editor-in-chief for Nupedia and later Wikipedia.[16][17] Nupedia was initially licensed under its own Nupedia Open Content License. Before Wikipedia was founded, Nupedia switched to the GNU Free Documentation License at the urging of Richard Stallman.[18] Wales is often credited with defining the goal of making a publicly editable encyclopedia,[19] while Sanger is credited with the strategy of using a wiki to reach that goal.[20] On January 10, 2001, Sanger proposed on the Nupedia mailing list to create a wiki as a "feeder" project for Nupedia.[21]

Launch and growth

Wikipedia was launched on January 15, 2001 (sometimes referred to as "Wikipedia Day"),[22] as a single English language edition with the domain name www.wikipedia.com,[23] and was announced by Sanger on the Nupedia mailing list.[19] The name, proposed by Sanger to forestall any potential damage to the Nupedia name,[24] originated from a blend of the words wiki and encyclopedia.[25][26] Wales stated that the idea for Wikipedia was influenced by the spontaneous order ideas associated with Friedrich Hayek and the Austrian School of economics after being exposed to these ideas by the libertarian economist Mark Thornton.[27][28] In particular, Wales was influenced by Hayek's essay The Use of Knowledge in Society stating it was "central" to his thinking about "how to manage the Wikipedia project".[28] Its integral policy of "neutral point of view" arose within its first year.[29] Otherwise, there were initially relatively few rules, and it operated independently of Nupedia.[19] Bomis originally intended for it to be a for-profit business.[30]

The Wikipedia home page on December 20, 2001[f]

Wikipedia gained early contributors from Nupedia, Slashdot postings, and web search engine indexing. Language editions were created beginning in March 2001, with a total of 161 in use by the end of 2004.[31][32] Nupedia and Wikipedia coexisted until the former's servers were taken down permanently in 2003, and its text was incorporated into Wikipedia. The English Wikipedia passed the mark of 2 million articles on September 9, 2007, making it the largest encyclopedia ever assembled, surpassing the Yongle Encyclopedia made in China during the Ming dynasty in 1408, which had held the record for almost 600 years.[33]

Due to fears of commercial advertising and lack of control, users of the Spanish Wikipedia forked from Wikipedia to create Enciclopedia Libre in February 2002.[34] Wales then announced that Wikipedia would not display advertisements and changed Wikipedia's domain from wikipedia.com to wikipedia.org.[35][36]

After an early period of exponential growth,[37] the growth rate of the English Wikipedia in terms of the numbers of new articles and of editors appears to have peaked around early 2007.[38] The edition reached 3 million articles in August 2009. Around 1,800 articles were added daily to the encyclopedia in 2006; by 2013 that average was roughly 800.[39] A team at the Palo Alto Research Center attributed this slowing of growth to "increased coordination and overhead costs, exclusion of newcomers, and resistance to new edits".[37] Others suggested that the growth flattened naturally because articles that could be called "low-hanging fruit"—topics that clearly merit an article—had already been created and built up extensively.[40][41][42]

In November 2009, a researcher at the Rey Juan Carlos University in Madrid, Spain, found that the English Wikipedia had lost 49,000 editors during the first three months of 2009; in comparison, it lost only 4,900 editors during the same period in 2008.[43][44] The Wall Street Journal cited the array of rules applied to editing and disputes related to such content among the reasons for this trend.[45] Wales disputed these claims in 2009, denying the decline and questioning the study's methodology.[46] Two years later, in 2011, he acknowledged a slight decline, noting a decrease from "a little more than 36,000 writers" in June 2010 to 35,800 in June 2011. In the same interview, he also claimed the number of editors was "stable and sustainable".[47] A 2013 MIT Technology Review article, "The Decline of Wikipedia", questioned this claim, reporting that since 2007 Wikipedia had lost a third of its volunteer editors, and suggesting that those remaining had focused increasingly on minutiae.[48] In July 2012, The Atlantic reported that the number of administrators was also in decline.[49] In November 2013, New York magazine stated, "Wikipedia, the sixth-most-used website, is facing an internal crisis."[50] The number of active English Wikipedia editors has since remained steady after a long period of decline.[51][52]

On January 20, 2014, Subodh Varma reporting for The Economic Times indicated that not only had Wikipedia's growth stalled, it "had lost nearly ten percent of its page views last year. There was a decline of about 2 billion between December 2012 and December 2013. Its most popular versions are leading the slide: page-views of the English Wikipedia declined by twelve percent, those of the German version slid by 17 percent and the Japanese version lost 9 percent."[53] Varma added, "While Wikipedia's managers think that this could be due to errors in counting, other experts feel that Google's Knowledge Graphs project launched last year may be gobbling up Wikipedia users."[53] When contacted on this matter, Clay Shirky, associate professor at New York University and fellow at Harvard's Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society said that he suspected much of the page-view decline was due to Knowledge Graphs, stating, "If you can get your question answered from the search page, you don't need to click [any further]."[53] By the end of December 2016, Wikipedia was ranked the fifth most popular website globally.[54] As of January 2023, 55,791 English Wikipedia articles have been cited 92,300 times in scholarly journals,[55] from which cloud computing was the most cited page.[56]

Sister projects
Main article: Wikimedia project

Wikipedia has spawned several sister projects, which are also wikis run by the Wikimedia Foundation. These other Wikimedia projects include Wiktionary, a dictionary project launched in December 2002,[57] Wikiquote, a collection of quotations created a week after Wikimedia launched,[58] Wikibooks, a collection of collaboratively written free textbooks and annotated texts,[59] Wikimedia Commons, a site devoted to free-knowledge multimedia,[60] Wikinews, for collaborative journalism[61] (which was later shut down in 2026[62]), and Wikiversity, a project for the creation of free learning materials and the provision of online learning activities.[63] Another sister project of Wikipedia, Wikispecies, is a catalog of all species, but is not open for public editing.[64] In 2012, Wikivoyage, an editable travel guide,[65] and Wikidata, an editable knowledge base, launched.[66]

Milestones
Cartogram showing number of articles in the top 88 Wikipedias (as of March 2024). The size of the circles for Wikipedias that have less than a million articles is fixed and not proportional to the size of the Wikipedia. The smallest Wikipedia that made the cutoff is the Haitian Creole Wikipedia with 69K articles.[g]
The languages are roughly grouped by region:

     Northern Europe          Eastern Europe     Middle East     East Asia     Indian subcontinent     Sub-Saharan Africa     Central Asia     Caribbean

In January 2007, Wikipedia first became one of the ten most popular websites in the United States, according to Comscore Networks.[67] With 42.9 million unique visitors, it was ranked ninth, surpassing The New York Times (No. 10) and Apple (No. 11).[67] This marked a significant increase over January 2006, when Wikipedia ranked 33rd, with around 18.3 million unique visitors.[68] In 2014, it received 8 billion page views every month.[69] On February 9, 2014, The New York Times reported that Wikipedia had 18 billion page views and nearly 500 million unique visitors a month, "according to the ratings firm comScore".[70] As of March 2023, it ranked sixth in popularity, according to Similarweb.[71] Jeff Loveland and Joseph Reagle argue that, in process, Wikipedia follows a long tradition of historical encyclopedias that have accumulated improvements piecemeal through "stigmergic accumulation".[72][73]

On January 18, 2012, the English Wikipedia participated in a series of coordinated protests against two proposed laws in the United States Congress—the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA) and the PROTECT IP Act (PIPA)—by blacking out its pages for 24 hours.[74] More than 162 million people viewed the blackout explanation page that temporarily replaced its content.[75][76]

In January 2013, 274301 Wikipedia, an asteroid, was named after Wikipedia;[77] in October 2014, Wikipedia was honored with the Wikipedia Monument;[78] and, in July 2015, 106 of the 7,473 700-page volumes of Wikipedia became available as Print Wikipedia.[79] In April 2019, an Israeli lunar lander, Beresheet, crash landed on the surface of the Moon carrying a copy of nearly all of the English Wikipedia engraved on thin nickel plates; experts say the plates likely survived the crash.[80][81] In June 2019, scientists reported that all 16 GB of article text from the English Wikipedia had been encoded into synthetic DNA.[82]

On January 18, 2023, Wikipedia debuted a new website redesign, called "Vector 2022".[83][84] It featured a redesigned menu bar, moving the table of contents to the left as a sidebar, and numerous changes in the locations of buttons like the language selection tool.[84][85] The update initially received backlash, most notably when editors of the Swahili Wikipedia unanimously voted to revert the changes.[83][86]

Both Sanger and Wales gave public interviews in late 2025 about their reflections about the status and state of Wikipedia, leading up to its 25 years of operation on January 15, 2026; Wales appeared on the PBS television news show GZERO World interviewed by Ian Bremmer[87] and Sanger has appeared on the Fox News Channel, interviewed by Ashley Rindsberg.[88] Wales' book The Seven Rules of Trust was published in October 2025 by Penguin Random House. It was described by the publisher as a "sweeping reflection on the global crisis of credibility and knowledge" with the book examining the "rules of trust" that enabled the growth and success of Wikipedia.[89]

Impacts of generative AI on Wikipedia views
Further information: Artificial intelligence in Wikimedia projects

Since January 2024, the Wikimedia Foundation has reported a roughly 50 percent increase in bandwidth use from downloads of multimedia content across its projects. According to the foundation, this growth is largely attributed to automated programs, or "scraper" bots, that collect large volumes of data from Wikimedia sites for use in training large language models and related applications.[90]

In October 2025, the Wikimedia Foundation reported an estimated 8 percent decline in traffic as compared to the same month in 2024 in human page views. They speculated that it reflects the growing use of generative AI and social media for finding information.[91][92]

Collaborative editing
Differences between versions of an article are highlighted.
Restrictions

Due to Wikipedia's increasing popularity, some editions, including the English version, have introduced editing restrictions for certain cases. For instance, on the English Wikipedia and some other language editions, only users with 10 edits that have an account that is four days old may create a new article.[93] On the English Wikipedia, among others, particularly controversial, sensitive, or vandalism-prone pages have been protected to varying degrees.[94] A frequently vandalized article can be "semi-protected" or "extended confirmed protected", meaning that only "autoconfirmed" or "extended confirmed" editors can modify it.[95] A particularly contentious article may be locked so that only administrators can make changes.[96] A 2021 article in the Columbia Journalism Review identified Wikipedia's page-protection policies as "perhaps the most important" means at its disposal to "regulate its market of ideas".[97] Wikipedia has delegated some functions to bots. Such algorithmic governance has an ease of implementation and scaling, though the automated rejection of edits may have contributed to a downturn in active Wikipedia editors.[98] Bots must be approved by the community before their tasks are implemented.[99]

In certain cases, all editors are allowed to submit modifications, but review is required for some editors, depending on certain conditions. For example, the German Wikipedia maintains "stable versions" of articles which have passed certain reviews.[100] Following protracted trials and community discussion, the English Wikipedia introduced the "pending changes" system in December 2012.[101] Under this system, new and unregistered users' edits to certain controversial or vandalism-prone articles are reviewed by established users before they are published.[102] However, restrictions on editing may reduce editor engagement as well as efforts to diversify the editing community.[103]

Articles related to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict are placed under extended-confirmed protection.[104] Editors also can make only one revert per day across the entire field and can be banned from editing related articles. These restrictions were introduced in 2008.[105] In January 2025, the Arbitration Committee introduced the "balanced editing restriction", which requires sanctioned users to devote only a third of their edits to articles related to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict even when no misconduct rules have been violated.[106][107]
